newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Tight soymeal underpins Europe but supplies on way.
newsitem.headline: Tight soymeal underpins Europe but supplies on way.

text.p: A perceived tight market in soybeans from the United States is expected to underpin physical prices here this week but traders are eyeing arrivals from South America which may decouple the European market, they say.
Early on Tuesday, European sellers were offering South American soymeal between unchanged and four dollars higher.
"The tight supply outlook in the U.S. kept pushing old crop beans up in Chicago and Europe followed," one trader said.

CBOT May soybean broke briefly above $9.00 a bushel for the first time since 1988 on Monday amid market speculation that next Monday's USDA crop report will show a further decline in ending stocks. The USDA in April put ending stocks at a tight 125 million bushels but estimates for the coming report are as low as 105 million bushels.
But European analysts are now wondering if this situation can last as a string of ships all carrying soymeal heads for the ports of Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Ghent.
According to shipping sources some 12 vessels, at least part laden with soymeal, will be docking in the next two weeks.
Market talk centres around some 200,000 tonnes of soymeal.

"We have had a tight supplies with sky-high prices to match but now with these arrivals there's too much for the current market to cope with," said analyst Arie van Dijk, analyst at market statisticians Stigevo.
Van Dijk sees these supplies as having a decoupling effect on European prices, freeing the market to some extent from what happens in Chicago.
"It could separate the markets. If prices continue to rise in Chicago, that will still be felt here but the influence will be much less," he said.
European compounders, reacting to high soymeal prices, have been lowering the percentage used in feed products, preferring ingredients such as rapeseedmeal and sunflowerseedmeal.
But there was now a change afoot, Van Dijk said, with compounders contemplating a switch back to South American meal.
The other main market issue was the weekend's heavy rain across Europe from northern Spain to northern Germany with forecasters predicting more on the way.
Analysts said the change in the weather had improved the prospects for the European grain crop.
"The drought has broken and people are now talking about normal yields for grains again," Van Dijk said.
But traders also noted that the market would be relatively quiet this week, slowed by the public holiday on Thursday in the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium.
"Buying will be slow in this broken week but it should pick up in the next two weeks," one said.
